title: The Reproducibility Crisis Incentive Structure
bottleneck: Researchers are rewarded for novel, positive results — not for verifying others' work — so replication studies are underfunded, underpublished, and career-neutral at best. High-profile failures to reproduce landmark findings recur across psychology, biomedicine, and machine learning, yet incentives barely shift. Journals reject most replication attempts as insufficiently novel, and funders rarely earmark money for verification.
why_it_blocks: An unreliable literature compounds: every downstream project built on a false result wastes resources and researcher-years. Fields with the weakest replication norms are often those guiding medical and policy decisions.
current_state: Registered Reports and replication journals exist but remain niche; funder mandates for reproducibility are mostly procedural. Large-scale replication projects have repeatedly found low reproducibility, yet the incentive structure barely budges.

sources.title: Evidence and the Design and Reform of Scientific Institutions (Nintil)
